headline.statement: The paper's second stated aim -- that emotion dysregulation mediates affect and loss-of-control eating differently across six eating dimensions -- is established only by which side of p = .05 each separately-fitted model landed on, and at the between-person level the coefficients called 'not significant' (0.89, 0.85) are LARGER than the one called significant (0.82).
headline.evidence: Table 2, between-person columns. Model 1, emotion dysregulation to LOC eating: 0.82 (0.41), p = 0.048, beta = 0.68 -- reported as a significant effect. Model 3, same path: 0.89 (0.46), p = 0.055, beta = 0.67 -- reported as 'not the difficulties stopping eating after starting ... at either level'. Model 1 indirect: 0.78 (0.40), p = 0.052 vs Model 3 indirect: 0.85 (0.45), p = 0.060. The paper's own table note fixes the threshold: 'Bold text is used to reflect significant effects, defined as p < 0.05'. No test of the difference between any two dimensions is reported anywhere.
headline.plain: The authors ran the same statistical model six times, once for each kind of loss-of-control eating, and concluded that emotion dysregulation matters for some kinds but not others. But they never directly tested whether any two kinds actually differ from each other -- they only noted which runs cleared the conventional cut-off for 'statistically significant'. In the between-person results the effect they call absent is actually slightly bigger than the effect they call present (0.89 versus 0.82); the only real difference is that one landed at p = 0.055 and the other at p = 0.048. The finding that these eating dimensions behave differently is therefore weaker than the paper presents it.

findings.title: Dimension-difference claim rests on threshold crossings, never on a test of difference
findings.location: Table 2 (between-person columns, Models 1 and 3); Results, 'Emotion Dysregulation (M) to LOC Eating (Y)' and 'Indirect Effects'; Discussion, 'Variations Across LOC Eating Dimensions'
findings.reported: Results: 'there were significant positive associations between the emotion dysregulation factors relative to the general sense of LOC while eating and feelings of disconnection ... at both the within-person and between-person levels ... but not the difficulties stopping eating after starting or the not paying attention to one's eating factors at either level.' Discussion: 'notable variations in this pattern of results emerged based on the LOC eating dimension under consideration.' Table 2 between-person: Model 1 emotion dysregulation to LOC eating 0.82 (0.41), p = 0.048; Model 3 same path 0.89 (0.46), p = 0.055; Model 1 indirect 0.78 (0.40), p = 0.052; Model 3 indirect 0.85 (0.45), p = 0.060.
findings.computed: absence_of_evidence on the Model 3 between-person path (b = 0.89, SE = 0.46) derives a 95% interval of [-0.012, 1.792] -- compatible with effects up to 1.79, on the same scale on which every between-person effect the paper reports as significant falls between 0.82 and 1.00. The tool returned severity `indeterminate` and declined to judge equivalence, because the paper states no smallest effect size of interest; its explanation is that 'no conclusion of no effect is licensed by these numbers alone'. Same structure for the Model 1 indirect path (b = 0.78, SE = 0.40; interval [-0.004, 1.564]) and the Model 3 indirect path (b = 0.85, SE = 0.45; interval [-0.032, 1.732]). Reading Table 2 directly, the point estimates ordered against the significance verdicts: 0.89 (called absent) > 0.82 (called present). Zero direct comparisons between dimensions are reported.
findings.assumptions: The derived intervals are b +/- 1.96 x SE on the normal scale; the paper prints no confidence interval and no degrees of freedom, so these are not the authors' own intervals and they inherit the two-decimal rounding of b and SE. The core observation -- that a coefficient called absent exceeds one called present -- needs no assumption beyond the paper's own printed table and its own stated alpha of .05. The framing that a difference between significant and non-significant is not itself significant is Gelman & Stern (2006), which I supply; the paper never claimed it. The innocent and near-universal explanation is conventional dichotomous reporting at alpha = .05, which is standard practice throughout this literature.

consequence.explanation: The paper's second stated aim -- 'variations in these associations across different LOC eating dimensions' -- and the Discussion's theoretical account of why some LOC stages are affect-driven and others are not, both rest entirely on comparing separate significance verdicts rather than on any test that two dimensions differ.

findings.plain: When you want to claim that something matters for one outcome but not another, you have to test whether the two outcomes actually differ. This paper instead ran a separate analysis for each of six eating behaviours and compared which ones cleared the usual significance cut-off. Two results landed on opposite sides of that line at p = 0.048 and p = 0.055 -- a hair's breadth apart -- and the paper treats them as different in kind, building several paragraphs of theory on the contrast. The numbers themselves point slightly the other way: the effect declared absent is the larger of the two. The paper's within-person findings for negative affect are not affected by this; the claim that dimensions behave differently is.

findings.title: Twenty-four mediational effects across six models, with no correction for multiplicity
findings.location: Table 2, Indirect effects rows, within-person and between-person columns, Models 1-6; Results, 'Indirect Effects'; Conclusions
findings.reported: Table 2 footnote: 'Bold text is used to reflect significant effects, defined as p < 0.05'. No correction for multiple comparisons is stated anywhere in the Statistical Analyses section or the table notes. Twelve within-person indirect effects (four significant as reported) and twelve between-person indirect effects (one significant as reported, p = 0.017) are presented from six models fitted to the same 107 participants.
findings.computed: multiplicity_report on the between-person family: 12 tests, family-wise error rate up to 46.0% if independent, about 0.6 false positives expected by chance. The single uncorrected significant result (p = 0.017) survives NONE of the four corrections -- 0 of 1 under Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli alike (Bonferroni threshold 0.0042; Benjamini-Yekutieli alpha 0.0161). n_claims_lost_to_correction = 1. On the within-person family the sweep computed the same 46.0% family-wise error rate, with 3 of 4 claimed effects surviving all four methods and n_claims_lost_to_correction = 1 -- the 'difficulties resisting eating' mediation at p = 0.026.
findings.assumptions: The family definition is my judgement: six LOC eating dimensions crossed with two affect predictors, all measured on the same 107 participants under one stated hypothesis. The paper never promised to correct for multiplicity, and uncorrected testing across outcomes is ordinary in this literature -- this is deterministic arithmetic about the reported p-values, not an allegation. Family-wise error rate assumes independence and is therefore an upper bound; these six outcomes come from the same people at the same moments and are certainly correlated, which is why Benjamini-Yekutieli is the appropriate reading. The paper also reports six further exploratory models on the same data in Data S1, so the true comparison count exceeds 24 and this is a floor.
findings.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --family-label 'Between-person indirect effects across 6 LOC eating dimensions x 2 affect predictors' --tests '[{"p_value":0.052,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.210,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.060,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.164,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.380,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.017,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.728,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.740,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.733,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.727,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.689,"correction_applied":"none"},{"p_value":0.725,"correction_applied":"none"}]' --alpha 0.05

consequence.explanation: The only between-person mediation the paper reports (negative affect to emotion dysregulation to feeling disconnected while eating, p = 0.017) survives no correction, yet it is stated as a substantive conclusion; the within-person mediation for 'difficulties resisting eating' (p = 0.026) also survives none, and is one of the four dimensions named in the Results, Discussion and Conclusions. The sole between-person mediation the paper reports (negative affect to emotion dysregulation to feeling disconnected while eating, p = .017) survives none of the four corrections, and it is stated in both the Results and the Conclusions. Computed from 1 result(s) significant uncorrected do not survive correction (a correction the paper did not apply, over a family we chose).

findings.plain: The authors tested the same idea two dozen times over -- six kinds of eating behaviour, two kinds of mood, at two levels of analysis -- and judged each test against the usual one-in-twenty cut-off without adjusting for how many tests they ran. Run twenty-four tests that way and you expect roughly one apparent finding from chance alone. Two of their reported findings sit close enough to the cut-off that they do not survive any of the four standard adjustments: the single between-person result, which they state as a conclusion, and one of the four within-person results. The other three within-person findings are strong enough (p = 0.001) to survive every adjustment, so the paper's central claim about negative affect is not in doubt -- but two of the specific claims built on top of it are.

findings.title: Six rows of Table 2 carry a mediation-path label under the 'Direct effects' heading
findings.location: Table 2, third 'Direct effects' row in each of Models 1-6, published XML version of record
findings.reported: In the published XML, the third Direct-effects row of every model is labelled 'Positive affect ➜ Emotion dysregulation ➜ LOC eating' -- verbatim identical to a row in the SAME model's 'Indirect effects' block that carries different numbers. Model 1: the Direct-effects row so labelled reads 0.28 (0.07), < 0.001, 0.13 within and 0.82 (0.41), 0.048, 0.68 between; the Indirect-effects row with the identical label reads -0.02 (0.01), 0.070, -0.01 within and -0.02 (0.05), 0.728, -0.02 between.
findings.computed: Read directly from get_table on the version-of-record XML, which reports alignment_uncertain: false and image_only: false, with spans_total = 8 (all model banners and header spans, correctly anchored) -- so this is the published label, not an extraction artefact. Three independent lines establish the intended label is 'Emotion dysregulation → LOC eating': (1) the NIH author manuscript prints exactly that for the same rows and the same numbers; (2) the Results narrative describes these very values as the emotion-dysregulation-to-LOC-eating direct effect -- 'within-person (beta = 0.13-0.14) and between-person (beta = 0.68-0.77)' matches Models 1 and 6 exactly; (3) Figure 1's path diagram specifies this path. Separately, a three-term mediation path cannot by definition be a direct effect, so the label contradicts the heading it sits under.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The contradiction is internal: the same label appears twice within one model carrying different numbers, and a three-term path is filed under a 'Direct effects' heading. The likeliest cause by far is a production or typesetting error at the publisher, not anything the authors did -- the author manuscript is correct.

consequence.explanation: A reader of the published version of record alone cannot correctly identify what six rows of the paper's central table report -- and those six rows carry the emotion-dysregulation-to-LOC-eating direct effects on which the paper's main narrative depends.

findings.plain: In the published online version, six rows of the paper's main results table are given the wrong name. They are labelled as though they show a three-step chain involving positive mood, but they actually show a single direct link between emotion dysregulation and loss-of-control eating -- and the wrong label is word-for-word the same as another row in the same block that shows completely different numbers. The numbers themselves are fine: every value I compared between the published version and the authors' own manuscript matched exactly. This is almost certainly a typesetting error introduced in production, but it means a reader of the published article cannot tell what six rows of the central table are reporting.

findings.title: No degrees of freedom, test statistic or confidence interval for any of Table 2's 84 coefficients
findings.location: Table 2, all 84 coefficients across Models 1-6 at both levels; Results, paragraph 1 (six LOC eating means and SDs)
findings.reported: Table 2 prints b, SE, p and a standardised beta for all 84 paths. No test statistic, no degrees of freedom and no confidence interval appears anywhere in the paper. The level-1 sample size -- the number of momentary observations that followed an eating episode -- is never reported; only 107 participants and 3131 completed surveys are given, and the LOC eating items were shown only to those who 'endorsed that they ate since their last survey'. The six LOC eating descriptives (e.g. 'general feeling of losing control while eating (M = 2.26, SD = 1.32)') are likewise reported with no n.
findings.computed: check_regression_batch: 71 coefficients submitted (13 omitted as 'p < 0.001' bounds), 0 evaluated, 71 indeterminate -- t cannot be converted to p without df. statcheck: 0 NHST statistics found in the prose, which is the correct result and not a tool failure; the paper contains no t(df), F(df1,df2), r(df), chi-squared(df) or z anywhere. Compounding this, b and SE are printed to two decimals, so for a row such as -0.07 (0.03) the implied Wald ratio spans roughly 1.86 to 3.00 and pins p only to about .003 to .063 -- a range straddling the paper's own .05 threshold. GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE could not be run on any of the six LOC descriptives for want of an n, though as single-item integer 1-5 responses they would otherwise be ideal candidates.
findings.assumptions: This is a refusal, not an accusation: nothing was checked, so nothing is impugned and nothing is confirmed. The reporting standard I am invoking -- that an inferential coefficient should be accompanied by enough information for a reader to reconcile its p-value -- is APA JARS-Quant (Appelbaum et al. 2018, Table 9) and is mine to supply; this paper claims no reporting guideline. Multilevel SEM software does not always print df in a single natural form, which is a real and partly innocent reason such tables often omit it.

consequence.explanation: Every inferential claim the paper makes rests on a p-value that no reader can reconcile against the point estimate and standard error printed beside it.

findings.plain: For each of the 84 statistical results in the main table, the authors give an estimate, a margin of error and a p-value, but not the extra piece of information a reader needs to check that the p-value follows from the other two -- and they never say how many individual survey moments the analysis actually used. The estimates are also rounded to two decimal places, which for the smaller ones leaves the p-value uncertain across a range that spans the significance cut-off in both directions. None of this means anything is wrong. It means that nothing in the paper's main table can be independently verified, which is unusual enough to be worth stating plainly.

findings.title: Survey compliance printed as 70.00% where 3131 of 4494 gives 69.67%
findings.reported: 'Participants responded to 3131 out of 4494 possible surveys, reflecting good compliance (70.00%).'
findings.computed: check_count_percent: 3131/4494 = 69.670672%, against a rounding interval for '70.00' of [69.995, 70.01]. Difference -0.33 percentage points. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 4472.9, which appears nowhere in the paper. The denominator itself is internally correct: 107 x 6 x 7 = 4494 exactly. The sweep verified the values are identical in the published XML and in the NIH author manuscript, so this is the paper's own figure and not an extraction or versioning artefact.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed numerator, denominator and percentage. Two innocent explanations carry real weight, and the first is likely: compliance may have been computed as the mean of per-participant compliance rates rather than the pooled ratio, and those genuinely differ. Against a simple rounding-to-a-convenient-figure explanation, the value is printed to two decimals, asserting four-significant-figure precision the pooled ratio does not support.

consequence.explanation: Affects only the descriptive characterisation of EMA compliance as '70.00%'; no inferential result depends on it.

findings.plain: The paper says participants completed 3131 of 4494 possible surveys, which it describes as 70.00% compliance. That division actually gives 69.67%. The gap is small and nothing in the results depends on it; the most likely explanation is that compliance was worked out by averaging each participant's own rate rather than dividing the two totals, which gives a slightly different answer. Worth a one-line clarification, not more.

findings.title: Trial registration number has seven digits and cannot resolve to any registration
findings.reported: 'The present study used baseline EMA data from a multisite randomized controlled trial (NCT0204349) testing the efficacy of Integrative Cognitive-Affective Therapy (ICAT-BED) versus guided self-help Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Eating Disorders (CBTgsh).'
findings.computed: The printed string carries seven digits after 'NCT'. ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers are 'NCT' followed by eight digits, so the string as printed denotes no registration. No arithmetic was performed; this is a reading of the document. The sweep verified the string appears identically in the published XML and on p. 6 of the author manuscript, so it is a typographical error carried through production rather than an extraction artefact. I have deliberately not guessed the intended number.
findings.assumptions: That ClinicalTrials.gov NCT identifiers are eight digits is a fixed property of the registry's identifier space, not a norm I am imposing on the paper; I could not confirm it against the registry in this session because this review reaches no network.

consequence.explanation: The parent trial's registration cannot be located from the identifier as printed, so a reader cannot check the registered design or outcomes of the trial that produced these data.

findings.plain: The paper identifies the trial its data come from by a registration number that is one digit short of a valid one, so typing it into the trial registry finds nothing. It is plainly a typing error rather than anything more, but it matters more than an ordinary typo because that number is the only pointer the paper gives to where its data came from and what the original trial said it would measure.

not_checked.location: Data S1 / Supplement (referenced nine times in the paper; not among the inputs supplied to this review)
not_checked.reason: The largest coverage gap here, and it is ours rather than the authors'. Data S1 is stated to contain the model fit statistics for all six MSEMs (the basis of 'All MSEMs exhibited good fit'), the multilevel confirmatory factor analyses confirming the factor structure of affect, emotion dysregulation and LOC eating, the missing-data analyses justifying the survey-number covariate, the comparison of the five excluded participants against the 107 retained, and the entire set of exploratory analyses. The authors deposited it; this review did not hold it. 'Present but not supplied to us' is not the same as 'absent'.

A full results section reports significance verdicts for a second set of six models with no coefficient, standard error or p-value in the main text -- those values are in Data S1, which we did not hold. Nothing in the section was checkable, and it means the paper's true multiple-comparison count is at least double the 24 tests I could enumerate.

not_checked.location: Table 1, BDI, CIA and DERS total-score rows (GRIMMER and SPRITE)
not_checked.reason: check_table refused these three cells by design: GRIMMER and SPRITE need a stated scale maximum and the paper gives none for any of the three instruments. Falling back on the tool's default 1-7 Likert range would manufacture an impossibility out of ordinary total scores. The SD of the BDI row (exactly 10.00, paired with a mean of exactly 15.00) is the one value in Table 1 I would most have liked to test and could not.

not_checked.location: Table 1, age, BMI and EDE global score dispersion values
not_checked.reason: check_sd_or_se returned indeterminate and was right to: the paper states no plausible range for age, BMI or the EDE global score, and inventing one would let an ordinary value be called implausible against a bound nobody published. Recorded so these three cells are visibly unchecked rather than silently counted as passing.

not_checked.location: Results, paragraph 1, six LOC eating means and SDs
not_checked.reason: Reported with no n. The denominator is the number of surveys that followed an eating episode, a subset of the 3131 completed surveys that is never stated, so GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE could not be run even though these are single-item integer 1-5 responses and would otherwise be ideal candidates. Only the SD-range check, which needs no n, applied -- and it passed against the paper's own stated 1-5 range.

The betas cannot be verified against the unstandardised coefficients without the latent factor variances at each level, which are not reported. They were read and recorded, but no check was run on them.

not_checked.location: Study Purpose, r = 0.948 between emotion dysregulation and negative urgency
not_checked.reason: Reported without n, df or confidence interval and attributed to a prior analysis of the same sample (Wonderlich et al. 2024), so no consistency check applies. Worth noting substantively rather than forensically: at r = 0.948 this paper's mediator and that prior paper's mediator are very nearly the same variable, which bears on how novel the present mediation result is.

Deliberately not run. The paper has one block of means and SDs (Table 1, a single sample), so there is no independent second block to compare. In Table 2 the 'Negative affect to Emotion dysregulation' row repeats near-identically across all six models, but that is expected, not duplication: the six models share the same predictor-to-mediator submodel on the same participants and differ only in the outcome. Supporting that reading, the between-person coefficient does vary across models (0.96, 0.96, 0.96, 0.95, 0.95, 0.95), exactly as re-estimation produces and copy-paste does not.

Not applicable and therefore not run. This is a single-arm secondary analysis with no treatment-arm comparison in Table 1, so there are no between-group baseline p-values to combine and the excess-similarity family of checks has nothing to operate on.

Not a finding, but recorded for the reader: data, materials and code are 'available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request' rather than deposited. This is an honest request-based statement, not the 'all data are included' pattern that signals evasion, but combined with our not holding Data S1 it means none of the fit statistics, factor analyses or exploratory results could be independently examined from what we had.

not_checked.location: table rows Baseline depressive symptoms (BDI total score), Baseline eating disorder-related clinical impairment (CIA total score), Baseline emotion dysregulation (DERS total score)
not_checked.reason: grimmer_check, sprite_reconstruct not run: this check needs a STATED scale maximum and the paper does not give one. It would otherwise fall back to a default 1-7 Likert scale, which for an unbounded variable manufactures an impossibility out of an ordinary value (measured: a mean of 35.78 members at n=64 reported `impossible` against an invented maximum of 7).

limitations: Figures WERE examined in this review. The paper contains one figure, a conceptual path diagram, which was located and cropped at high confidence and read: it depicts model structure (lagging, levels, X/M/Y roles) and carries no axes, no plotted data and no error bars. No statistic in this paper is reachable only through a figure, so the usual figure-blindness caveat is not a live gap here.

This system reads one paper and reaches no network. Two questions a reader needs in order to weigh these findings are outside its reach entirely: whether similar patterns appear in other papers by the same authors, and how the equivalent values compare against other studies in this literature. Both are open to the reader, not settled by this report.

check_effect_plausibility holds no citable benchmark row for momentary multilevel mediation coefficients in ecological momentary assessment research, so the effect-size plausibility dimension was UNAVAILABLE for this paper. I did not substitute a neighbouring field's benchmark or my own impression of what counts as large.

The three intervals underlying finding 1 were derived by this review (b +/- 1.96 x SE on the normal scale, no df being available), not printed by the paper. They inherit the two-decimal rounding of the coefficients they come from and are approximate to that precision.
The registration-identifier finding rests on the eight-digit format of ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers, which I could not confirm against the registry itself because no network was reachable.

The multiplicity result depends on a family definition that is my judgement, not the authors'. Grouped differently -- for instance treating each LOC dimension as its own family -- the arithmetic changes.

Table 2 (Multilevel structural equation models) -- 84 coefficients across 6 models x 2 levels; 71 submitted to regression-batch and all indeterminate for want of df; 21 rows cross-checked against the PDF; all 60 rows re-read at source in this stage

questions_for_authors.question: In Table 2 of the published article, the third row under 'Direct effects' in each of Models 1-6 is labelled 'Positive affect ➜ Emotion dysregulation ➜ LOC eating' -- the same wording as a row in the same model's 'Indirect effects' block, which carries different values. In Model 1 the Direct-effects row so labelled reads 0.28 (0.07), p < 0.001, beta = 0.13 within-person and 0.82 (0.41), p = 0.048, beta = 0.68 between-person. Could you confirm that these six rows report the emotion dysregulation to LOC eating direct effect, as the Results narrative and Figure 1 indicate?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles whether the published label is a production error and whether the version of record misidentifies six rows of the central table.

questions_for_authors.question: Table 2 reports b, SE, p and a standardised beta for all 84 paths but no degrees of freedom, test statistic or confidence interval. Could you send the degrees of freedom (or the test statistics) for the paths reported in Table 2, together with the level-1 sample size -- the number of momentary observations following an eating episode that entered each model?
questions_for_authors.why: Would make the paper's inferential results independently reconcilable; at present no reported p-value can be checked against its own coefficient and standard error, and the level-1 denominator is unstated.

questions_for_authors.question: The Results state that emotion dysregulation was associated with the general LOC while eating dimension (between-person b = 0.82, SE = 0.41, p = 0.048) but not with difficulties stopping eating after starting (b = 0.89, SE = 0.46, p = 0.055). Did you run any formal test of whether these two coefficients differ from one another -- for example a joint model with the LOC dimensions as a within-participant factor -- and if so could you send the result?
questions_for_authors.why: The paper's second stated aim is that mediation varies across LOC eating dimensions; that claim currently rests on separate significance verdicts rather than a test of difference, with the larger point estimate on the non-significant side.

questions_for_authors.question: The Results report 3131 of 4494 possible surveys as 70.00% compliance, where the pooled ratio gives 69.67%. Was the 70.00% figure computed as the mean of participants' individual compliance rates rather than as the pooled ratio?
questions_for_authors.why: Distinguishes a different and legitimate denominator from a rounding or transcription slip.

questions_for_authors.question: The parent trial is cited as NCT0204349, which carries seven digits where ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers carry eight. Could you supply the full registration number so the trial's registered design and outcomes can be located?
questions_for_authors.why: The identifier as printed does not resolve, and it is the paper's only pointer to the provenance and registered design of the data analysed.

report_markdown:
## What the paper claims

This is a secondary analysis of baseline ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data from a multisite randomised trial of two binge-eating-disorder treatments. One hundred and seven adults with BED completed up to six brief surveys a day for seven days. The authors fit six two-level multilevel structural equation models asking whether momentary emotion dysregulation mediates the path from momentary negative and positive affect to each of six distinct loss-of-control (LOC) eating dimensions -- a general sense of losing control, difficulty resisting eating, difficulty stopping, feeling driven to eat, inattention, and feeling disconnected. The headline conclusions are that emotion dysregulation mediates the negative-affect route to several LOC dimensions but not others, that no pathway involving positive affect was significant, and that these patterns differ meaningfully between the within-person and between-person levels.

No treatment arms are compared anywhere in this paper, so the baseline-similarity family of checks -- normally the first move on a trial's Table 1, and the one where uniformly high p-values are the red flag rather than reassurance -- has nothing to operate on here. I did not run it, and its absence is not a gap.

## What verified

Where exact arithmetic can reach this paper, it holds up well. Every one of the fifteen count-and-percentage pairs in Table 1 reproduces to the last printed digit over N = 107. All three categorical blocks -- gender, education, race/ethnicity -- account for exactly 107 participants with no tolerance at all, and the sample flow reconciles exactly (112 enrolled, 5 excluded, 107 analysed). The three instrument total scores are reachable as integer sums over 107. The six LOC eating standard deviations all sit inside the 1-5 range the paper itself states, checked against the paper's own bound rather than one I supplied. And on the twenty-one Table 2 rows where the published XML and the authors' own manuscript overlap, every coefficient, standard error, p-value and standardised beta matches to the last digit; the only difference is the leading-zero convention. Twenty-one of the checks that ran came back consistent, fifteen of them collapsed inside a single table sweep. That is what a carefully prepared descriptive table looks like, and it is worth saying so: nothing in Table 1 is impugned.

One sweep flag I have removed. Three Table 1 rows were initially marked suspicious because their implied sums exceeded a 1-7 Likert maximum -- but that ceiling was a tool default, not the paper's, and a Beck Depression Inventory or DERS total is obviously not a 1-7 variable. The granularity test itself passed on all three. Resting a finding on a bound the paper never stated is exactly what the rulebook forbids, so those three are consistent.

## Where the difficulty lies

The problems that survive are not arithmetic. They are about what the reported numbers can support, and they cluster into two.

The first is inferential. Two dozen mediational effects were tested against a single conventional threshold with no adjustment, and the two results closest to that threshold do not survive any of the four standard corrections -- including the sole between-person mediation, which the paper states as a conclusion. Uncorrected testing is ordinary in this literature and I do not treat it as a defect of these authors; the arithmetic is nonetheless what it is. More consequentially, the paper's second stated aim is supported by comparing which separately-fitted models cleared the threshold, never by testing whether any two dimensions differ -- and the coefficients point mildly against the conclusion drawn from them.

The second is verifiability. Not one of the 84 coefficients in Table 2 can be reconciled against its own p-value, because no degrees of freedom, test statistic or confidence interval appears anywhere, and the number of momentary observations actually entering the models is never stated. Statcheck found zero recomputable statistics in the prose, which is the correct result and the same gap seen from a second angle. This is a refusal, not an accusation: nothing here is shown to be wrong. But a reader who wants to check the paper's inferential claims against its own printed estimates cannot do so at any point.

Three residual items -- a compliance percentage that does not match its own numerator and denominator, a seven-digit trial registration number, and six mislabelled rows in the published version of the central table -- are small individually. The mislabelling is the one worth the publisher's attention, since the author manuscript has it right and the version of record does not.

## Trust

The descriptive statistics in this paper reconcile cleanly and the strongest within-person findings survive every correction I applied, so the core claim -- that momentary negative affect predicts loss-of-control eating through emotion dysregulation -- stands on its own numbers. What does not stand as stated is the narrower claim that this process differs across types of loss-of-control eating, and the single between-person conclusion. I would treat the paper's main finding as sound and its dimension-by-dimension distinctions as unestablished pending the model fit statistics and the degrees of freedom.
